transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

Occupational health sent me. They think I’m not eating enough. Most days it’s black coffee, maybe a plain yogurt, and a few bites of chicken at night. A full meal just feels like I’m letting my standards slip.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?
Yes. If the scale’s up even half a pound, I get this jolt—like I’ve lost control. Then I cut back harder the rest of the day. I can’t stand the thought of putting weight back on.
Do you get unwanted thoughts about food or your body that feel intrusive and hard to dismiss?
I’m not sure what you mean by intrusive. I do think about my weight and what I’ve eaten a lot, but it doesn’t feel out of nowhere to me.
Does your weight have a big effect on how you feel about yourself as a person?

Yeah, it does. When I look in the mirror, I zero in on my stomach and waist. If I don’t look lean enough, it affects how I see myself for the whole day—whether I feel like I deserve any respect, really.

I don’t know the exact number right now. My uniform hangs off me, and I’ve had to tighten my belt past the old notches. The nurse said it was dangerously low, but honestly, I still thought I could stand to be a little sharper.

This rules against atypical anorexia and other unspecified/other eating disorders.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports marked dietary restriction with very low intake, intense fear of weight gain, increased restriction in response to minor scale increases, and self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape/weight. Despite being told their weight is dangerously low and noting loose clothing/belt tightening, they still believe they could be leaner, indicating disturbed body image and poor recognition of the seriousness of low body weight. This presentation is most consistent with anorexia nervosa.
